syllabus.clause: doubling with amortized cost vs incremental migration across two tables (Redis dict) to bound per-operation latency

at.step: Doubling pays for the whole rehash in one insert, proportional to the table's current size.
Redis's own dict keeps both the old and new table live, and migrates entries a few at a time instead of all at once.
Incremental migration's bound caps every single operation's cost, no matter how large the table.
Incremental migration keeps both tables live for many operations, not one — a real, sustained memory cost for a smoother latency.

items.item: A second hash table is prepared for incremental rehashing; both tables stay live during migration

items.item: A rehashing step moves a bounded number of buckets, and caps how many empty buckets it will scan, so no single operation blocks unboundedly

sources.source: This curriculum's own aggregate-method proof (Ch.1/Ch.2), cited not re-derived

items.item: Doubling gives O(1) amortized cost per insert by the aggregate method — the same argument already proved for a growable array, now applied to rehashing

at.step: Doubling pays for the whole rehash in one insert, proportional to the table's current size.

items.item: Every collision scheme built in this chapter so far assumed the table already had room; this topic is the one all three previous topics quietly deferred — what happens when it doesn't.

at.step: Every scheme in this chapter has worked inside a table of fixed size. None of them has said what happens when that table fills up.

items.item: Doubling's amortized O(1) cost per insert is the same aggregate-method argument already proved for a growable array's reallocation, now applied to rehashing (a genuinely different cost than copying, since every key's slot can change) instead of copying.

at.step: Doubling pays for the whole rehash in one insert, proportional to the table's current size.

items.item: Averaged over many inserts, doubling is cheap — but the one insert that actually triggers the rehash is not; its cost scales with the table's current size, not a constant.

at.step: That one insert — how does its cost compare to an ordinary insert right next to it?

items.item: Redis's own dict answers the same question differently: keep the old and new table both live, and migrate entries gradually instead of pausing to move them all at once.

at.step: Redis's own dict keeps both the old and new table live, and migrates entries a few at a time instead of all at once.

items.item: Migration isn't a separate background process — it's called from inside the dictionary's own ordinary lookup and insert operations, riding along on work the table was already doing.

at.step: Who actually moves those keys from the old table to the new one?

items.item: A single incremental-migration step is bounded by design (caps both buckets moved and empty buckets scanned), so no one operation ever pays for the whole migration, regardless of table size.

at.step: Incremental migration's bound caps every single operation's cost, no matter how large the table.

items.item: Incremental migration is not a free lunch: both tables stay live for the whole migration, a real, sustained memory cost that lasts far longer than doubling's single rehashing insert.

at.step: Incremental migration keeps both tables live for many operations, not one — a real, sustained memory cost for a smoother latency.

items.item: Both resize strategies move the same total number of entries across the same sequence of resizes — the difference is entirely about the schedule each one pays on, not the total amount of work.

Redis's own dict has a concrete, named minimum-fill threshold (1/8 occupancy) below which it becomes willing to shrink — a real, cited number for 'hash tables under memory pressure,' not an invented one.

Concurrent or lock-free resizing (migrating a table that multiple threads touch at once) is a real, harder version of this problem, named with no mechanism, since the syllabus doesn't name it for this topic.

at.out: Syllabus names only doubling, incremental migration, and memory pressure for this topic — concurrent/lock-free resizing is not named, so it's left as a named-only frontier item.

items.item: This topic's own measured numbers (worst-op cost, total work, migration duration) come from a from-scratch table built in examples.py, not from Redis's own real-world benchmarked performance, which this topic makes no claim about.
